In the eerie silence of the swamp, Jess was brutally murdered with a sai, leaving Detective Winston sorting through a mire of secrets and lies involving two prime suspects - Leona and Freya.

Winston looked out at the swamp that had claimed Jess's life. Following the cordoned path, the flash of evidence markers catching his eyes, he ran his fingers around the sai in his hand. It was of a unique make, identical to the style used in Freya's martial arts training and not commonly found. There were not many who could handle such a unique weapon, fewer still who owned them.

The path led him to Freya's home later that day. He was introduced into a crisp and clean living room, save for an empty slot in a display case filled with a fascinating collection of sais. He pondered silently, looking at the missing gap, like a puzzle awaiting to be solved, surely it must have been an important sai to her.

Off the bat, Freya seemed uncomfortable as she started nervously, "It's good to see you detective, I’m sure you've heard from my friends, they stopped by and I expressed to them my concerns about Jess threating to disclose my secrets. They comforted me, assuring me they would speak to her.”

Seeing that Freya seemed distressed, Winston decided to breach the topic divertedly, “Freya, I notice one is missing. Care to tell about it?”

With a hesitant nod, Freya spoke, “It recently went missing. The one missing held a sentimental value to me, Detective.”

"Picked up any replacements?" He asked. “Any practicing recently?”

"Well, I was at my dojo last week for training," Freya offered.

An⟦ interesting⟧ tidbit given the recent events. He was drawn by a peculiar object on a side table. A phone, separate from the one Freya had nervously returned to her pocket.

“This your personal phone, Freya?” Winston asked.

Freya’s cheeks reddened, and she quickly replied, “That's my private phone, detective. I find it easier to keep my personal lines separated from the world.” The device was quickly turned off, secure under her watchful gaze.

Throughout the conversation, she seemed uncomfortable whenever he moved too close to anything personal, quickly steering to another topic. Noted, Winston thought, but he was yet to bring up anything about Jess.

“Freya, let me cut to the chase. Jess was found to have written a letter to the local paper about exposing someone's dark secrets. We found a large payment from you to a private investigator. Want to tell me something?"

She seemed aghast. "Detective, Jess had been saying for a while that she had something on me that could ruin me. But we all have our secrets, don’t we? I hired someone to figure out what she had, it was all in my defense!”

Winston took a moment to consider her words. She was a charming woman, but he was trained to look past faces. "It's good to be honest, Freya," he added quietly, placing the sai back in the evidence bag and heading for the door. 

Once back in his car, he noted how stalwartly Freya switched off her private phone when he was around, an action that made him ponder as he started his vehicle to return to base.

Winston had never been a huge fan of pop music, he preferred jazz. Nevertheless, he found himself standing next to a stage that had, the previous night, been vibrating with the sound waves of Leona's music. Leona, a young singer with a dazzling voice that had jetted her to national stardom. Now, just twenty-four hours after her astonishing concert, she was being questioned by Winston, a detective, about the horrific discovery that morning of Jess' lifeless body beside the neighboring swamp.

He found Leona backstage, looking distraught.

"Your concert last night," Winston spoke patiently. "The venue was right next to the swamp, am I correct?”

Leona, with her tear-stained mascara, nodded. "Yes, detective. It was."

"And you had Jess present? Jess with the VIP pass?"

"Yes," Leona replied, her usually confident voice reduced to a mere whisper. "She even met my sister after the show."

"Interesting," Winston muttered, trying to keep his tone neutral. "Because I had a report that she was seen arguing with your sister. She seemed rather threatened."

Leona's face was a mask of sadness as she recalled the event. "My sister? Threatened? I...I saw it happen, she looked scared during their confrontation. Later, Jess also sent a threatening message to my sister after that confrontation. It really upset her and she's been in a distressed state since then."

Noticing the grim determination on Leona's face as her thoughts drifted to her sister, Winston probed further. "I heard you're protective of her," he added, watching Leona's reaction.

Visibly shaken, Leona admitted, "I always have been." She dabbed at her eyes with a tissue. "We only have each other. That's why I didn't object when she wanted to come to my martial arts classes."

"Ah, your martial arts classes," Winston interjected. "I have on my record here that you've been seen attending those regularly over the past months."

Leona looked surprised. "Yes, detective. I needed a way to vent out my stress, and I found martial arts comforting."

"Martial arts, hmm?" Winston mused aloud. "Your instructor even mentioned that you've been progressing quite well and he admires your skill with certain weapons. Have you ever handled a sai?"

Fear was written clear on Leona's face as she quietly nodded, understanding where this conversation might be leading to. "Yes, I have. I just purchased a set and have been training with them. They stay in the dojo, though. I swear.”

Little did Leona know, but her confession perfectly fit the narrative Winston was trying to weave. He gave nothing away with his stoic expression.

"I heard," he continued slowly, "that after the concert, Jess was seen headed towards the swamp."

She nodded her head, "Yeah, people sometimes take that route to avoid the traffic..."

The conversation ended, and Winston didn’t probe further. As far as Detective Winston was concerned, he had all the information he needed. He had many clues to ponder over and a murder investigation to lead. The image of the sai next to Jess's body in the swamp was quick to return as he went back to his car.<turn|>

I was inside the local café, mulling over the case when I saw Autumn. She was a regular here, always engrossed in a murder mystery novel, which somehow comforted me in a way. Detective work made you appreciate the mundane things about life.

"Autumn," I greeted her as I approached, "how are things?" 

She took a moment, reached down into her bag, and pulled out a specific thrilling novel titled "Perfect Crime". She glanced up from the book and responded, "Oh, hello Winston. Just the usual."

I looked down at her book, the title striking a chord, "This one any good?"

Autumn got excited and spoke in vivid detail about the perfect crime plotted in the novel. Her enthusiasm around the theme of crime and the specific details almost perturbed me, but I chose to focus on the dialogue at hand.

We mentioned Donald, and how he had plans⟦ to⟧ head to the bunker. Autumn froze for a moment before returning to her normal composure. "He trusted you," I said, "would have let you in the bunker."

"The bunker? Yeah, I know the place. Donald used to talk about it," she replied, trying to sound nonchalant. But I could discern a hint of unease in her voice, the knowledge of the bunker and everything that had transpired there appeared to weigh heavy on her.

Autumn had been in a gang with Donald. Back in the day, they used to own this town, running around and kicking up dust wherever they went. Time moved on, things had changed, but the past lingered in Autumn's fear of her past crimes revealing themselves.

Donald had confided in me once that he discovered Autumn was still engaging in criminal activities. She had psychic abilities which made her an asset in their criminal past and perhaps, in her current endeavours.

The clang of the door brought me back to the café. Autumn had left, the sunshine reflected off her hair as she headed down the street, her murder mystery novel tucked securely under her arm. The people in the café moved again, life resumed while questions circled in my mind. Along with Autumn, I left the café: one looking to uphold justice, and the other, potentially, to evade it.

Winston walked down the long, subterranean corridor again, guiding his flashlight along the intricately detailed blueprints of the bunker he held in his hands - blueprints that once belonged to the experienced Jay. Once housed in the station, this giant underground maze was a known territory to Jay, of course, but to Winston, it was all foreign.

Hours later, in a makeshift interrogation center in the surface barracks, Winston eyed the familiar face of the missionary, Jay.

"I've seen the blueprints, Jay," he said simply, watching the other man's face.

"Oh, those?" Jay replied, a light airiness showing in his reply. "I spent quite a bit of time down there when I was stationed at this bunker. I could still walk through it blindfolded."

"And isolated…" Winston added, his gaze never leaving Jay's face. It was a known fact that the underground bunker locked from the inside and the only two keys existed – one with Donald and the other with Jay. It had been established earlier that Jay and Donald were the only ones inside the fortified bunker during the time of Donald's death.

Jay didn't respond immediately. He looked disinterested, detached. He finally spoke up, "I guess Donald had started to suspect, huh? He confronted me about it a few days ago."

"You've done some snake handling, haven't you?" - Winston asked.

Jay chuckled. "A rite of passage, they call it. Over there in the region with a high snake population, it’s a trial, a blessing, an exorcism.” His tone held a grim, respectful distance. 

Winston nodded, "I've heard it's common among missionaries to learn about snakebite remedies as well."

"A living antidote, in case of a bite, that's not common knowledge."- Jay answered, leaning back in his chair.

"Were you aware, Jay," Winston began, "that Donald discovered certain… irregularities?"

Jay's eyes flickered to Winston's for the first time. "Irregularities? You mean the smuggling?" He admitted.

Winston let the confession hang in the air between them.

"I was using the missions to distribute certain substances, that part is true." Jay said.

"You got trained here, in the bunker. Now you distribute substances, in religious ruse. " His tone turned pointedly menacing. 

He leaned in slightly, resting his elbows on the tabletop, "Discovery of which, Jay, would do a lot more than tarnish a reputation."

Jay remained silent, his eyes hardening and body rigid, awaiting the impending threat the detective presented. 

Winston suddenly backed off, taking his notes and exiting the room, leaving Jay alone among his thoughts.<turn|>

In the quiet solitude of a local library, Philip is found shockingly murdered with a barbed wire, leaving Detective Winston with the arduous task of sifting truth from alibis of the two main suspects, Hugo and Maria.

Winston's mind was buzzing during the ride to the local hair salon, a tragic incident sinking his spirits. Philip, a library frequenter, was dead, with dire circumstances suggesting a gruesome murder. The weapon, a coil of barbed wire, unusual for sure. As he walked into the salon, he saw a middle-aged woman, Maria with a multitude of barbed hairpins reflecting ominously under the lights. She was working away with a pair of scissors, her nimble fingers managing both the razor and the various hairpins with the dexterity of an artist.

"Maria?" Winston asked.

Caught off guard, Maria looked up, her eyes wide in surprise. "Yes, detective, can I help you with something?" she answered, never pausing her delicate dance of grooming. She clicked her scissors, moved on to her razor, then her infamous collection of barbed hairpins, all with the practiced ease of someone in her profession for a long time. 

"I hear you've been doing this for over fifteen years?" he asked, partially making small talk, partially feeling out the woman in front of him.

"Sixteen years, next Tuesday." She replied, her gaze deliberately focused on her current client's head. 

"Quite a long time..." Winston said, thoughtful. "You ever do hair for a fellow called Philip?"

Maria paused for a moment, her eyes downcast. "Yes, I did his hair once. He's the one found in the library, right?"

"Yes," Winston nodded, "I heard about your usual evening strolls to the library. The one open late till 10 pm?"

"Yeah, it's quiet, peaceful. They don't mind if I bring my coffee inside. I even have a key, just in case I lose track of time and it's closing," Maria disclosed.

"I see. How about Robert? Phillip's fiance. He been here, recently?" Winston changed the subject.

Maria swallowed and cleared her throat, stepping away from her customer to face Winston. "Yes, he came... to talk." 

"To talk about the wedding, or about that time in high school where you confessed your love to him before he proposed to Philip?" Winston probed.

Maria averted her eyes, "About the wedding... but, yes, we also brought up the past. I've been in love with Robert since high school, and I've been secretly carrying that love for years, you know."

Winston observed Maria. Things certainly aren't always as they seem, he thought, as she returned to her client, her barbed hairpins dancing in the slightly unsettling light. The fact that the time of Philip's death aligned eerily with Maria's usual library visit was an added layer of unease. "Well, Robert's supposed to marry Philip soon, isn't he?" 

"Yes, but things aren't always as they seem, detective." Maria's voice held an edge as she responded, her gaze being both hurt yet defiant, hinting at a deeper tale yet to unravel.

Blowing off steam, jumping from coffee shop to coffee shop, Winston was back on track, unanswered questions regarding Philip's mysterious murder bouncing in his mind. Known for his capacity for violence to get what he wanted, Philip had a reputation; ironically, barbed wire, his common form of conflict resolution, had been the weapon.

The detectives at the precinct were all a twitter about the eccentric sound technician, Hugo. Out of all potential suspects they'd drawn in, one thing about Hugo was blinking on Winston's radar. Not once had any colleague, friend or customer ever been invited to his personal studio where Hugo spent most of his time. The man was protective of his private space, it seemed. 

"I'm detouring to Hugo's office," Winston informed his partner as he made a left turn.

The professional layout of Hugo's studio stood testament to his skills. Winston noticed the different⟦ categories⟧ of wires neatly stowed away, labeled by type. Spools of common wires were neatly packed, then his gaze floated towards an unusual collection of unique wires, barbed wire included, labeled 'personal collection'. He stroked one with his gloved fingers, lost in thought.

"Hugo," Winston called for his attention, "This is some impressive collection. Not everyone works with barbed wire in a sound system, huh?" Hugo's smile was gentle, "I just like to keep my wire knowledge versatile," he shrugged.

"I heard you missed out on this year's industry conference," Winston inquired casually. 

"Yeah. Conferences are not my cup of tea," Hugo chuckled, "Too much show and too little know. I prefer focusing on the actual job, here in my studio."

Casual chat moved reflective as Winston asked about Philip, "What about Philip? Ever get into a formal tussle with him?" Hugo's rifle through a box of cables paused, "No direct confrontation, sir, but I was an unfortunate audience to threats he made to my brother over a phone call. Nastiest conversation ever."

Winston nodded, taking in the distraught sound engineer before himself. Hugo's brother owed a significant amount to Philip, everyone and their nephew knew that. It had been no blind gamble, but rather a bet gone awry. It had complicated Hugo's personal dynamics, certainly. Especially so since no one saw Hugo at the annual company holiday party. Usually a regular, Hugo's absence sent alerts.

Duty kept Hugo traveling between different venues for sound gigs, with a vast array of tools tagging all along, wires included, also, wires very similar to the ones found at Philip's crime scene. Winston mulled over this kaleidoscope of details, knowing well the devil lay in their details, as he drove back to the precinct.<turn|>

In the wake of a gruesome flamethrower murder at a local soccer field, seasoned detective Winston steps up to investigate, with suspects Sophia and Larry under his watchful eye.


"Detective Winston," Sophia greeted as she shuffled her cardboard coffee cup in her hands nervously. They were standing on the edge of the football field where the murder had taken place.

"Sophia," Winston nodded, looking out at the half-time huddle of sweaty, tired players - the same scene where Savannah had taken her last breath. 

Sophia was a journalist. She'd been covering the match when Savannah was killed, following her usual line of reportage. Today, she'd been on the field, right where it all happened. Savannah's murder had occurred right at halftime and yet, nobody seemed to know anything. 

"So, it's been a while since your reports on the military exhibition, correct?" Winston asked, keeping his face calm but watchful to catch any change in her expression.

"Yeah,  it was a couple of months ago. I still have the flamethrower I'd managed to keep, for research and, you know... reminders," Sophia said, her gaze flickering toward the field. 

Winston nodded. He knew that keeping memorabilia wasn't uncommon in her trade. Did it provide Sophia with a flamethrower when she needed one?

"Savannah, were you two friends?" Winston asked, keeping an eye on the middle of the field where everything had happened.

"We knew each other... She threatened to reveal my source, ruin my credibility," Sophia sighed, staring at her untouched coffee. 

Sophia's job was at stake, Winston knew; in a field like journalism, credibility mattered.

"Why didn't you tell anyone about the threat?" 

Sophia shifted uncomfortably, "I had heavily invested time and energy in this article. I was protecting my...trust in the field. My source was my lifeline." 

Winston didn't reply but noted her skittishness in revealing her source even now.

"Look, the match is starting!" Sophia pointed out to the field as the whistle blew.

Winston just nodded, eyeing the field where the murder had taken place. If he was to solve this case, he had to sift through the evidence slowly and carefully. Even when it came from a journalist faced with the threat of losing her job and credibility. Even when it was wrapped up in the middle of a football game.

Winston crunched on a stale coffee flavoured donut while wiping away the grim remnants from the computer monitor in his rundown office. He had been staring at the sport section of the local newspaper that spoke about the location of the unfortunate demise of Savannah, a keen enthusiast and promoter of sports in the city, especially soccer who also happened to be a strong opponent of Larry in politics. 

The photograph of the soccer field was chilling, almost like a badly done modern graffiti that had charcoalled the grass in obscene patterns. A flamethrower had been the murder weapon and such a trait of weaponry could point to only a certain group of people who had the experience to⟦ operate⟧ such a complicated tool of destruction, typically war veterans, like Larry.

Larry lived in a secluded house surrounded by woods, and held his position as head of a local survivalist group. Very often, his colleagues complained of Larry turning off his phone and avoiding them after work. This lack of response to text messages, calls, or any other means of digital communication could only be explained by Larry's choice to retreat in solidarity and bare minimal social contact. 

Winston sighed, pushed away the paper, and prepared to visit Larry. As usual, in unsociable fashion, Larry declined Winston's invitation to join his colleagues. 

Winston knocked on the rustic door of Larry's eerie looking cabin. When Larry opened the door, he looked like he had just finished a drill. He was sweating, hair a disheveled mess, his posture was rigid and alert. His eyes darted to his wristwatch, hinting towards a habit that he exhibited during various events, checking time frequently. "Larry," Winston said.

Larry recognised him and invited him in albeit reluctantly. A quick glance around the room was enough to see survivalist instincts visible in every corner. In amongst the survival gear was a flamethrower, a common item found in survivalists tool kits. But Winston ignored it and tried to talk politics. 

Larry seemed keen to steer the conversation towards Savannah - his fiery political rival. Winston learned Larry had a habit of attending all the political rallies personally. Savannah's recent rally was public, held downtown at the center square, and as always, Larry had been present. 

Trying to make Larry more comfortable, Winston asked Larry about his social life and why he declined invitations to join others. Larry just shrugged, avoided Winston's gaze, and said he wasn't interested in what others were doing.

His answers lacked conviction, but Winston held his professionalism and didn't push any further. He thanked Larry for his time and left.<turn|>

In the wake of Lola's mysterious katana-driven demise at a secluded mountain cabin, Detective Winston finds himself entangled in a web of suspicion, with Isabelle and Frank peering anxiously from its corners.

Winston gazed contemplatively at a mountain cabin photo where Lola had met her end. He grimaced as his gaze landed on the katana. This was not a run-of-the-mill crime; it was seemingly conducted with a professional touch.

Bringing himself back from the troubling images, he turned his attention to Isabelle. As Lola's life coach, she could potentially shed some light on the complexities surrounding her death. 

Flicking novel-like through an accumulation of notes, he discovered that Isabelle was not as open as most coaches. She engaged with her clients predominantly through privacy-focused platforms and kept any personal details off public forums. The agreement she held with her clients also contained a clause about prioritizing privacy and confiding in her seemed to be one of her requirements, and David --the other man Lola had an affair with-- was no exception. He confided in her, quite frequently as it turned out.

However, what caught his attention was a note hinting at her discovery of intimate text messages between Lola and another man. That's why she confided uneasily with David more, ushering them into lengthy personal conversations and extraneous time spent alone. They had far more interactions outside the coaching sessions than was typical.

Pulling into Isabelle's driveway, Winston noticed the peace that surrounded her home. Inside, Isabelle waited patiently on an austere chair, a sharp contrast to the decor of the rest of the home.

"Busy day?" A plain, professional question to start off with. 

"Indeed. Three sessions at the Dojo and then some client interactions," Isabelle replied. 

"Wow, that's a tight routine. At the Dojo, I assume you work with the Katana?" Winston tried to keep his tone casual.

"That's correct. I try to keep them in the best condition... sharpening included."

Her house was decidedly sparse, but one room was markedly different. A room dedicated to her treasured collection of Katana. Delicate, sharp, deadly works of art.

Isabelle was not one to engage unnecessarily; she had expressed as much. But there was one occasion where she did seem to talk, quite a bit actually. To David.

"Have you met David outside of the coaching sessions?" Winston asked, as he examined one of the Katanas. 

"Yes, a few times. Our schedules happen to coincide," she responded, her eyes averted.

"And some of these encounters were in regards to the intimate messages Lola was sharing with the other man?"

"Yes, that's correct."

"In connection with Lola, perhaps?"

Isabelle's gaze hardened. "Lola was stepping over boundaries - I saw her kissing David."

The session ended with more questions than answers for Winston. He casually bid her goodbye, having established she preferred minimal social interactions.

"Gotta head back, Isabelle, can't keep the precinct waiting. You have a good day now." He put on his hat and walked out, leaving Isabelle with her thoughts.

Detective Winston sat hunched over his quaint oak desk, his dark eyes scanning⟦ over⟧ the phone records of the deceased, Lola. He jotted down a quick note - Lola had dialed one number numerous times, the number belonging to a certain Frank. It seemed Lola made a habit of contacting him.

His notes also mentioned that multiple witnesses had recently spotted Frank practicing with his Katanas at a local martial arts studio. His swordsmanship had certainly improved, it showed dedication.

The following day, Winston found himself driving up the mountain to meet with Frank, a well-respected biologist having an impressive and crucially vital academic career. Frank's workspace was littered with numerous awards and commendations highlighting the value of his work; it was clear that his reputation was important to him.

"Good afternoon, Frank," Detective Winston greeted, extending a hand.

Frank looked up from his microscope and shook the detective's hand, "Afternoon, detective. What brings you here?"

"Lola invited you to her cabin under the semblance of a work retreat, isn't it?" Winston asked, leaning against the lab desk.

"Yes," Frank replied reluctantly, "But I never told anyone else about that."

Winston nodded and changed the topic, grabbing one of the photos off the table. It was shot a few days ago, Lola and Frank seemed to be in a heated discussion, "Care to share what this altercation was about?"

"Nothing serious, just some professional disagreements," Frank dismissed hurriedly, seeming eager to move past the topic.

As Winston glanced around the room, he noticed something else; A pair of katanas meticulously maintained and displayed on the wall. "You have an interest in martial arts, Frank?"

Frank seemed to relax a little, leaning back from the microscope, "Yes, I've been taking classes recently. It helps me focus."

"And what about these?" Winston asked, indicating towards the Katanas.

"Ah those..." Frank trailed off. "Well yes, I've been practicing with them, they're my favorite weapon of choice in martial arts," he admitted, quickly adding, "but they're only for practice."

Winston headed to the local hardware store after the meeting to confirm another fact. Frank had indeed bought a sharpening stone just a couple of days ago.

At the end of the day, he checked out Frank's public schedule - it was free on the day Lola got murdered, just as his hunch had indicated. He cross-checked with some bystanders, who also confirmed seeing Frank near the mountain cabin on the same day.

As Winston wrapped up his day of investigation, he couldn't help but remember the one last crucial piece of information. Lola had been blackmailing Frank with evidence of academic misconduct, tarnishing the career he was so proud of.<turn|>

When fitness enthusiast Uma is ominously murdered with a vial of acid at her local gym, it's up to seasoned Detective Winston to unravel the mystery between the two prime suspects, Irving and Addison.

Detective Winston was indoors on another stifling California afternoon. His attention was fixed on the Irving case, a case that kept him on his toes for several days now. A screenwriter suspected in the murder of a fellow gym goer. He couldn’t help but feel the increasing pressure of the time crunch.

Irving was not an ordinary man. Winston had discovered from the interviews and police records that the guy particularly had some weird habits. Irving, it seemed, was battling insomnia and was unable to sleep in his own home at night. During these restless nights, he would busy himself with his notebooks. Often, he was seen at the fitness center, sketching intriguing symbols into his notebook, which he always carried along with his pencil. He would leave home with these immediately after sunset.

One specific detail that struck the detective was Irving's fascination with themes and symbols of the past, particularly those formed by ancient gravestones. These ancient symbols were found in notations and sketches strewn across his notebooks. It was curious to Winston how an old world art found a home in the hands of a modern screenwriter.

His insomniac late-night habits weren't the only thing that raised suspicions, though. Irving also was a member at the same fitness center Uma frequented, spotted regularly training late into the night. The very same fitness center that was the scene of the crime. The records substantiated his presence late on the night of the murder. Like the deceased Uma, he seemed to utilized the solitude that the near-empty gym provided, allowing him ample time alone.

The lines on Winston's forehead became more pronounced as he read on. He found a strange connection between both Uma's and Irving's lives. Not only did they work out at the same gym, but they also shared a professional conflict. Reports indicated that Uma had discovered Irving's success was largely built on her own work which he'd plagiarized. Fearing public humiliation and the definite demise of his screenwriting career, Irving had a lot to lose. To make matters worse for Irving, Uma, the aggrieved, had threatened to expose his deceit to the public.

The tension of the case was truly weighing on Winston. He sighed, leaning back from his desk. Questions in his mind demanded answers that weren't there yet. So, he decided to continue with the investigation, waiting for the breakthrough that would add some clarity to the clouded picture. He had a late-night meeting with the prime suspect, Irving, in the pipeline. It was indeed time to probe further and extract some answers from the silence of the night.

Detective Winston admired the modern glow of the fitness center that served as his next stop in the investigation. The thudding of footfalls on running machines, the humming of weight machines, and the faint scent of sweat and disinfectant whispered of a place that had teetered on the edge of life and death.

"Lookin' to join?" came a voice from behind him. He languidly turned to find Addison, the local trainer.

"No. Detective Winston, on official police business," he presented his badge.

The sour taste of surprise was evident on Addison's face, "We're an excellent gym with a friendly vibe; it's a shame. You don't say, a detective?"

"I've checked the fitness center security cameras," Winston watched as Addison pressed his lips together, "Noticed you were entering the gym shortly before time of Uma's death."

Addison placed a hand on a weight machine, lowering his gaze to his feet. "Uma? You mean my client, Uma? We were scheduled for a training session that day."

Winston opened his notebook, scanning his notes, "You have a background in chemistry, is that right?"

Addison looked up from his shoes, "Yeah, I even teach it at the high school. Possess a chemistry degree and recently purchased a chemistry set for demonstration."

"Interesting. The set contains vials of acid, science class protocol?" Winston asked, his brow furrowing.

"Absolutely, controlled experiments to teach risk and safety," Addison said, transported into the world of academia. The detective noticed a flicker in Addison’s expression as he continued to speak but brushed it off, it meant nothing yet.

A few people from the gym had crowded around now. They watched as Winston asked, "Can you recall Uma saying anything about the honesty of the staff or maybe about any missing equipment?"

"Well," Addison began, rubbing his neck, "Uma did once vouch for me, said I was honest and commendable, a good character, you know." He looked around the room and swallowed. "And yes, she did mention once about missing equipment. Unfortunately, she also stumbled upon some CCTV footage of me taking some expensive equipment. I had intended to return it, it was a mistake. "

As Winston watched the gym members disperse, he looked back at Addison. "So, Uma caught you stealing from the fitness center. That must've been uncomfortable for you. It surfaced in the investigation that fitness equipment has been reported missing recently. Uma seemed to have discovered the theft."

Addison suddenly seemed to find the floor tiles fascinating. "Uma was a good woman," he said quietly. "It's a shame what happened to her."

"Agreed," Winston replied, closing his notebook. "Keep a clear schedule, Addison. We'll be in touch."

As Winston exited the gym he took one more glance at Addison through the large glass panes. Cold air nipped at his face and Winston pondered the car ride back to the station.<turn|>

In the hushed sanctity of a mosque, Kent falls victim to a deadly snake venom, leaving Detective Winston with two prime suspects: Ronald and Julia.

Cold sweat trickled down Winston’s spine as he perused the grim photos of the crime scene at the mosque. Winston fished the statement reports from his pile of case files, which stated that Kent and Julia were last seen together at the mosque.  Kent had been poisoned with snake venom, a tricky murder weapon to trace. His victim, Kent, was Julia's cousin and had last been seen at the mosque with her before he met his unfortunate fate.

His next stop was clear. He pulled his coat close against the biting wind and snow. Silicon Valley, estate of one Julia. Inside, he found Julia embroiled in what seemed an exhaustive pile of legal documents. From their exchange, he learned that she was currently tangled up in a knotty lawsuit, where the opposing party had a good deal to gain, financially that is.

Stepping into what he could only describe as a mini laboratory, a brave new world peered back at him. Labeled samples cluttered the table, one of which was a snake venom sample. Julia was trained as a herpetologist and her job involved working with venomous snakes, she explained this to Winston while also showing him her work with venomous snakes.

As they moved⟦ past⟧ countless terrariums, Winston paused in front of a portrait on the mantel. “That’s Kent,” Julia sighed. “Always the favored one, especially by Grandpa. In his latest will, everything was left to him. The will was initially expected to be in my favor, but, he bypassed me completely," Julia said. Her voice turned bitter as she revealed these shocking discoveries about her cousin, Kent.

Changing the topic to something less contentious, she mentioned that both of them used to frequent the same mosque for prayers, the very place where Kent was last seen alive by people, before she added, "And we were together at the mosque that same day." Her tone hardened as she described an altercation with Kent she had had earlier that day at the mosque. The tension was palpable as she revealed her own cousin had been secretly helping the opposition in the ongoing legal battle.

Winston nodded, took a few final notes, and bid his farewell, a gust of wind blowing in with the opening of the front door. His footsteps crunched the snow beneath his boots and the stark contrast of his solitary car in the vast white providence painted an odd yet mystic picture. As he drove off, the silhouette of Julia’s house receded, but the flicker of suspicion stayed kindled in his mind.

Winston sauntered into the buzzing fairgrounds. His worn Panama hat tilted, casting a shadow over his contoured face as he surveyed the spectacle of the annual town fair. Ronald, the man he had come to see, was easy to spot - standing tall in his uniform as security for the event.

"Ronald?" Winston called out after weaving through the crowd of cotton-candy eaters and parched parents.

A sharp look from Ronald confirmed his identity.

Ever the expert at concealing his hand, Winston lightly grazed the topic. "I hear you’re pretty experienced with snakes. Handle 'em at the zoo, right? A zoo with quite a variety of venomous snakes, so I've heard."

A flicker of pride sparked in Ronald's eyes. "Yes, that's right. From rattlers to mambas, we have them all. I have the keys to all animal enclosures, even the Venomous Serpent Exhibit."

"Must be quite a job, wrangling all those snakes," said Winston. "Especially with the variety of venomous species you have. They can be lethal with their venom."

"You bet. But it's all about understanding and respect," Ronald’s eyes reflected the love for his job.

That’s when Winston changed tactics. He didn't have the luxury of time; the fair was busy, and he sensed Ronald wouldn't stay guard at his post for long. 

"I need to talk about some documents," he said. Before he even finished his sentence, the color drained from Ronald’s face. "Documents linking you to past misdemeanors. They were found on a man named Kent."

The denial came swift and in violence. "This is preposterous! That man was maligning me; I did nothing wrong!”

A shrill kiddy ride whirled inches from them, momentarily deafening Winston to anything else Ronald had to say. By the time the wooden cars clattered to a stop, Ronald was sprinting the other way. 

He was no longer at his post, no longer within sight, and no longer within Winston’s reach for further questions. For now. The detective adjusted his hat, scanning the field. Winston knew he had started unraveling traces, but he’d need to tread carefully here on out. Ronald was spooked, and even the deadliest snake wouldn't strike unless cornered.<turn|>

Winston was sitting in his car, gazing at the misty country road that led to Gordon's farm. Bad news was often paired with a country farm, but today was particularly grave - A death at the chalet, a bear trap, and a farmer named Gordon.

Winston spotted a shotgun in a corner, a disturbing sight considering it was the same type specified in the coroner's report for Isaac's death. It was an intriguing piece of evidence, considering Milton owns the shotgun.

Their conversation veered into various topics, with Milton highlighting his passion for reading. His bookshelf was lined with an extensive collection of books on death rituals from around the world - yet another proof of his peculiar interests. 

In the midst of their conversation, Isaac's name came up. Following reliable sources, Winston knew something crucial - Isaac had stumbled upon evidence directly implicating Milton in a tax evasion scheme. Isaac, the ever-vigilant whistleblower, was preparing to expose Milton's scandalous scheme - a revelation that could land Milton in prison.

As Winston left the fitness center, he pondered on his findings. Milton's tax evasion scheme, his interest in funeral practices, the shotgun license, the matching murder weapon... it all seemed to connect. He was confident that the tax evasion evidence would be enough to send Milton to jail, but for now, only time would tell. It was just another day on the job for Winston. As for Milton, his fate hung in the balance.

Winston approached Alice cautiously and asked, "You know Isaac's workout routine, correct? The list of Isaac's routines you've given us earlier... it matches the information we gathered. You both were here all the time."

Alice was quick to correct him, "Not to boast, Winston, but I've been handling such arms ever since my military days."

The troubling image of the man in the photos, nunchaku in hand, in a laser tag arena was threading an unsettling narrative through Winston's mind. Perhaps he'd taken the martial arts fascination a step too far? Or had too much of a stake in a possible payout from an insurance policy? 

Winston recalled his earlier conversation with Timothy. "So, you're quite the laser tag enthusiast," he'd mentioned casually. Winston walked his fingers over the glossy crime scene photos spread out before him. The soccer field, typically a place of good-hearted competition and family fun, had been turned into a spectacle of horror as Ivy met her untimely end. The only saving grace was that the game had been called off before the tragedy unfolded.

Ivy was a frequent attendee of these games, often seen happily sipping on a cold drink from the stand. This time, it had been her undoing.

Winston was no rookie, but cases like these sent a cold shiver up his spine. Putting the photos back into the case file, it was time to pay Hugo a visit. 

Hugo was perched on a stool in the recording booth when Winston arrived. Despite the match being called off, Hugo had been working as a sound engineer at the same match. His work as a sound engineer was only a few blocks away from the matchplex, it was a stone throw away. Working with sound engineering also meant that Hugo had to handle chemicals regularly as part of his job role. Winston noticed a tattoo peeking from the arms of Hugo's rolled-up flannel – the name Anna, inked with what seemed like a real sense of devotion.

"Hugo?" Winston asked, leaning against the doorframe.

"That's me," Hugo replied, his eyes never leaving the windows of his booth.

"I hear you were serving refreshments at the match yesterday," Winston said, trying to keep his tone neutral.

"I was, yeah," Hugo confirmed with a nod, "I often help out there."

"You've been seen leaving work that day, "Winston continued.

"Yeah, I left to go set up the refreshments," Hugo responded.

At first glance, Hugo didn’t seem like the type who would care about a toxicology course, but records indicated he had taken one in the past. Moreover, his work required him to handle complex sound equipment which could involve frequent contact with certain chemicals.

Winston circled back to Hugo's protective side. "You seem close to Anna."

"Yeah," Hugo’s gaze softened, "hee, she's like my baby sister. I've always looked out for her."

Any detective worth his salt knew how protective bonds could drive people to extreme lengths. Winston had heard from others about some cruel remarks Ivy made about ruining Anna and of threats to press charges against her. 

"All right Hugo," Winston said, throwing his coat over his arm, "thank you for your time."

Winston had more pieces to the puzzle now, but he knew the killer wouldn't reveal himself easily. Winston, as always, would be waiting patiently. After all, a game of cat and mouse was half the thrill of his job.

Winston's latest case had piqued his curiosity, leading him to a popular coffee shop downtown where Ivy, the person of interest, was a regular. As he strolled in, the distinct aroma of dark roasted beans permeated the air. Behind the counter, Meredith worked with great efficiency amidst the morning rush.

From a nearby television, a clip replayed on the local news – Ivy, laughing boister⟦ously⟧ whilst imitating some sacred rituals, unmistakenly disrespecting Meredith's beliefs. Today was no exception. As she prepared for her work day, her fingers grazed her amulets and she muttered a silent prayer before diving into the morning pandemonium.

Meredith often spoke publicly about being a staunch follower of her religion and openly declared – more times than Winston would care to count – that anyone who disrespects her beliefs deserves severe punishment.

In the midst of the bustling shop, Winston's attention was drawn to a framed photograph. Meredith was captured mid-spit, a chicken wing in hand.

"But she only buys raw meat," the butcher's words echoed in his mind, contrary to the image he was witnessing. He recalled Meredith’s friends' words: "Meredith has never had cooked meat in front of us."

He paused, glancing around the rink, then asked, "Do you know how they got in? The murderer, I mean."

Winston frowned slightly, "During the game," he answered, watching Justin's face carefully. He appeared unphased.

Justin cocked a brow, excitement mixed with intrigue evident in his lit eyes. "I was here during that time," he pointed out, "Watching the game."

Winston nodded, "You were, and as far as anyone knows, you didn't leave until well after," he almost sighed, "Listen Justin, what exactly is it with you and this crime? It seems that you're more interested in it than the hockey game."

Justin shifted, looking anywhere but at him, "Well, it's just...Marvin and his fiancé, you know. I just thought they...weren't right for each other. I had a talk with her once. I asked her not to marry him. But she didn't listen."

Winston's nose wrinkled as he entered a home office that had been marred with blood and remnants of barbed wire. Whispers of Isolde's last moments — what had she seen, what had she felt — clung to the air, making Winston's skin cling to the white collar of his shirt. 

A key piece of Isolde's life had been her role in exposing medical malpractice. Video evidence, meticulously collected, strangely presented itself beyond the crime scene. She had been building a case against Samuel, a man Winston was becoming increasingly interested in. 

Samuel had been a paramedic, receiving intense training which even included handling emergency situations with injuries from barbed wire. The unfortunate ironic nature of his education was not lost on Winston. He was a man trained to save lives, to handle emergencies. But there had been a serious error during a previous medical procedure, an error Samuel found hard to live down. Now, he made his living in a medical supply store, trying to make up for lost time, perhaps. 

One sunny Monday, Winston himself had seen Samuel, sunglasses shading his eyes, his job posing no hindrance to his apparent penchant for intrigue. Just the next day, the sunglasses had been replaced with eyeglasses. That was a curious detail — Samuel didn't have a prescription for eyewear.

Intriguing, things left to ponder. 

As for the barbed wire, that vile instrument's origin led back to a storage unit. Samuel had a key to said unit. Had he known about its contents? It was, after all, not a common item for city dwellers to come by. 

Then, there was the matter of the hair. Samuel, a typical brown-haired man, had recently been seen sporting hair as dark as the night. A local store clerk had mentioned selling black hair dye to a man fitting Samuel's description days prior. 

Winston remembered mutterings of a superior warning Samuel about potential job loss even jail time. The detective felt a chill run down his spine as he processed the connections. 

A visit to Samuel was in order. 

Similar to sirens he responded to, Samuel generated a certain kind of alarm in Winston's mind too. It was time to figure out who was saving lives and who was ending them. Perhaps, sometimes, they were one and the same, Winston couldn't help but consider as he headed to interview the paramedic, and potential suspect, Samuel.

Winston was a weathered detective who had seen it all, or so he thought, until he was handed his latest case - the murder of Isolde. The crime scene was none other than her shared home office with her partner, Bernard. The fatal weapon, strangely ominous, was a strand of barbed wire.

Winston was aware of one crucial information piece; Bernard's regular grumbles about Isolde's monopoly over the crime territories. A monopoly Bernard would have liked to gain control of, no less. Detective Winston flicked through the reports once again. The guy is a dock worker, moved shipping containers around all day. It was a harmless hobby, but it didn't sit right.

"The dock's a rough place, Winston," said Officer Daniels, a baby-faced officer with a knack of not following orders, "You can't be weak and thrive there."

"I bet Frederick's co-workers would tell you about his strength and dexterity. Cargo isn't a walk in the park," Winston said, taking in Daniels' recommendation. Strength and dexterity... it reminded him of something. The weapon, a sai, was found in Frederick's collection.

Winston rubbed his brow lightly and continued turning the pages. Frederick was a devotee of warfare artifacts. From ancient katana to modern assault rifles, Frederick had them all. 

"Frederick goes for racing during his free time," the report read. In fact, suspicious activity at the go-kart track was often reported around Frederick's usual racing time. Winston remembered Frederick's racing schedule: every Thursday at six, without fail.

On the day Gary was killed, Frederick and Gary were both at the go-kart track. Gary, a joker at heart, was seen messing around with Frederick's go-kart, the very same one that Frederick had previously confronted others about.

Winston sighed, leaning back in his chair. Daniels had a defensive glance in his eye.

"But he's just an enthusiast! And skilled, I heard," Daniels defended, almost pleadingly. 

Winston only nodded, his mind already spinning with strategies and weak alibis. 

"He's also a dockworker, known for his strength and dexterity, able to handle heavy cargo safely." He paused. "Isn't a sai a pretty lightweight weapon?"

"Yes sir." Daniels stuttered out, not daring to look Winston in the eye. "Frederick..." he swallowed. "Frederick might have the skill to wield a sai."

Winston continued reviewing the reports and evidence, his mind far from eased, his heart heavy with the task at hand. The dockworker. The go-kart track. The sai. The confrontations over the go-kart. The timelines adding up just so... Suspicions were nothing until proven in the court of law. But still, it was a start. Time to pay Frederick a visit.

Clouds hovered above the go-kart track as Winston surveyed the murder scene. The sight of Gary's lifeless body had been replaced by yellow police tape, but the stain of what had occurred remained imprinted in Winston's mind.

Indisputably, Gary was the current go-kart champion of their small town. A title that endowed him a sense of invincibility and an obstacle for Jerome, the runner up more times than Jerome cared to admit.

Winston pulled the collar of his coat up, glancing around the track at the groups of people, all huddled up and whispering.⟦ Among⟧ the crowd, his eyes locked onto a man standing alone, pressing binoculars to his eyes. His attention constantly straying elsewhere, ears tilted towards passing conversations as if eavesdropping. Winston couldn’t help but notice the insular behavior of the man.

"You're Jerome, right?" Winston asked. The man gave him a nod, his gaze fixed on the distant track. Jerome's listless eyes betrayed not apathy but a high passion for go-karting.

Jerome and Gary shared this passion, Winston learned, their go-kart rivalry was quite the spectacle in the local area. Contentious races, frequently ending with Gary taking the championship title very heatedly debated, and it was just a week ago when Gary accused Jerome of cheating.

"In his own world, isn't he?" commented one of the local racers, watching Winston's attempt to engage Jerome. "I've heard them arguing a lot recently. Especially after the last race..." he glanced at the silent Jerome.

Winston noted to visit the local gym, where Jerome had been seen practicing fight moves occasionally. The man was known to have a certificate of martial arts mastery as well. That singled him out, especially considering the nature of the murder weapon, a sai.

Thinking of sai, a cold wave of realization spread through him. He had seen a receipt in Jerome's office for multiple such weapons, and rumor had it that Jerome had been spotted purchasing multiple sais only a week back.

As the evening wind picked up, Winston took one last look at the solitary figure of Jerome. He was engrossed in his own world even in a crowded gathering. Suspicion, it would seem, wore many masks. It was time, Winston decided, to uncover the truth.<turn|>

In the heart of a bustling fitness center, Heidi's life was abruptly silenced by a shotgun's blast; now it's up to the astute Detective Winston to round up suspects Grace and Chester and unravel the threads of this complex murder mystery.

Winston studied Grace's appearance as she labored over the dismantling of her shotgun, a routine she performed with a kind of measured grace that only came with practice.

"I take it hunting is a regular hobby of yours, Grace?" he asked. She straightened her back and brushed a lock of hair from her eyes, her hands still loosely holding the dismantled firearm. She nodded.

"It's tradition. Heidi and I would always go out into the wilderness, me with my nine-two shotgun, her with her ridiculous tin of marshmallows. I remember she'd always be the one who'd leave, while I'd stay at the fire, peering into the forest, not returning to the tent." Grace chuckled, but her smile didn't reach her eyes. "Even when we were out here, pushing fitness, she was looking out for safety."

"And you had a mutual workout routine both of you followed?" Winston questioned.

"Yes, every day like clockwork." She sighed. "But I convinced Heidi to change it. I argued it was safer, better for her. That night she was murdered, she implemented the change."

Winston looked at her, his sharp eyes noticing the glimmers of distress in hers. "Could that change have caused her to meet her killer?"

"She started seeing someone. I thought it was best if we changed the time, to throw off this new person. But she didn't listen..." Her voice held a slight edge, possessive almost.

As she related the details about her trips with Heidi, Winston noticed her rain-soaked hiking boots, mud-streaked pants, and her tired eyes.

"Looks like you've been out there yourself today?" he gestured at her appearance.

"Busy day," Grace responded curtly, her gaze never leaving the shotgun she was now starting to reassemble. "I usually got up the earliest. Not much point in sleeping when there's hunting to be done. The guys in the camp aren't morning people anyway."

"I see," Winston muttered, "You two, you worked out together frequently, didn't you?" 

"Heidi's the one who introduced me to working out at the fitness center. We would even do so late at night, just us, a lot of sweat and a hell of a lot of heavy lifting." She smiled at the thought, her eyes glossing over with a mixture of remembrance and grief. 

Winston nodded, scribbled down a few lines in his notepad and thanked her for her time. There was still so much to understand, so much to link together.

Sunlight filtered in through the windows of the fitness center, casting long shadows on the equipment and machines scattered around the vast room. In the corner of the spacious gym, Chester was spotted, tending to some weights when detective Winston walked in.

Chester, slight in stature, belied his physical prowess as a jockey. His wiry exterior seemed incongruent with the voracious power emanated by his presence. "Hello Chester," Winston began, his gruff voice noticeably contrasting with the calmness of the gym.

"Detective Winston, isn't it?" Chester replied with ease, his demeanor not showing a single shred of surprise or fear. Just two weeks ago, Chester had started⟦ his⟧ new gig at the fitness center, partly to make some extra bucks and partly to maintain his fitness routine. It wasn't surprising to Winston that Chester would frequently show up right when Heidi, an active member of the gym, was last seen alive.

Just when he had started to become regular at the gym, murmurs among Chester's gang had grown louder. They've started questioning his loyalties, not convinced that his regular visits to the gym were purely for maintaining his fitness.  

Their subtle talk was interrupted by the loud reverberations of gunshots in the distant background. Chester, an avid hunter, often flexed his shooting skills at the range nearby after winding up work at the gym.

"You like to shoot, huh?" Winston casually pointed towards the direction of the gun shot sounds. "Yeah. Helps take the edge off," Chester replied, a faint smile appeasing his otherwise-hardened face.

The conversation gradually led them to Heidi, a brave woman who had recently made criticisms about Chester's gang at a local town meeting. Their illegal activities were an open secret in town, countered only by the fear they instilled in those who dared to oppose. Heidi was the latest in the list, her fate tying in with an unfortunate coincidence: Chester's gang members are known to carry shotguns, the same kind that ended her life. 

Detective Winston and Chester finally diverged to their respective routines. The detective's mind was buzzing with theories, but his face was an ocean of calm. He had gathered the facts. The story had to be spun. His job could not be influenced by hasty conclusions... not when the facts all led to one presumable as intimidating as Chester.<turn|>

Detective Winston regarded the lone figure sitting before him across the table. Richard’s face was absorbed in the glow of the paused true crime documentary, his eyes reflecting morbid fascination and intense concentration.

"Just finishing up your work-out?" Winston asked, gesturing towards the sweat-soaked shirt.

"Ah, yes, detective," Richard confessed, catching on to his implication. "Those marks? I was practicing my nunchaku techniques in the martial arts class before you arrived. Quite challenging to get the swings right. Purchased these nunchaku from a sports equipment store last month. It's part of my martial arts training."

"Martial arts? I wouldn’t have expected that from a waiter," Winston said, conversing readily.

"The mosque I work at, it's next to this martial arts institution. We do nunchaku⟦ training⟧ as part of our drills. Isabella, tragically enough, was also a part of the same class, and I just like keeping myself engaged." Richard shrugged.

"Speaking of keeping engaged," Winston glanced towards the paused documentary on the laptop, "Looks like you've got quite the fascination with true crime, huh?"

"I listen, rewind, analyze, and repeat..." Richard said, reaching towards his notebook that lay next to the computer, brimming with his own investigation strategies, "I write down interesting details. I find it... intriguing, to say the least."

"Ah, a keen observer. Useful in a job like yours," Winston said, nodding in understanding. 

"I rarely interact with anyone outside my working hours, detective," Richard asserted with a hint of defensiveness, immediately finishing off his sentence. "The day the tragedy happened, I was at the martial arts class first, then I went to the mosque...but I was alone."

The glint in Richard's eyes gave away nothing, but Winston saw the flicker of insight deepen. With a curt nod, he stood up, leaving Richard in the expanse of his own silence. As the day drew to a close, Winston had to acknowledge one thing - Richard was an enigma, much like the case he found himself entangled in.

Detective Winston was having one hell of a day, nursing a mug of coffee that had long since turned cold with the reports strewn about on his desk.

The door cracked open, revealing a man infamous in the neighborhood not only for getting into altercations with people of other races but also for his often vocalized hatred for racial diversity. His slightly frazzled appearance, a telltale sign of his usual state after the stress of an intense composing session, was something that Winston had been briefed about.

Rex didn't take long to proudly discuss them, speaking about their age and antiquity. He mentioned having picked them up from an auction recently.

"These from one of those crossbow shooting classes you attended?" Winston asked casually, nodding at the collection.

In between the conversation, Rex shared about his love for music, how he had built the studio with his own hands, and made the deliberate decision to not include a restroom. He also revealed why he spent most of his free time here - he had no other hobbies outside of the studio.

Once they wound up, Rex seemed even more restless, fidgeting with the sleeve of his sweater, an increased sign of stress after their conversation. Winston thanked the man for his cooperation and took his leave. As he left, he couldn't help but take a mental sweep of the meeting.

In the chilling silence of a serene campground, Ernest meets his untimely end by a crowbar; now, it's up to the keen instincts of Detective Winston to unravel the mystery with only two suspects: Addison and Octavia.

Winston found himself by the cars. Addison, the mechanic apprentice, was working under the car hood. He flipped through a book that was on a nearby table while working. Every time he paused to point out something in the room, like the faded motivational posters on the wall or the cozy layout of the waiting area, Winston chuckled. Addison always had an eye for room decor.

"Hard at work I see." Winston said, breaking the silence. 

Addison shut the book and turned to face him. "The work never ends," he replied, looking Winston up and down. 

"I hear you were at the same camping site as Ernest. He was found murdered there." Winston shared. 

"Work, school, camping... always busy." Addison replied, his gaze wandering again. He'd developed a habit - one even his fellow students noticed during lunch breaks and in every class - of constantly looking around at different parts of the room. 

Winston noticed that tendency walked hand in hand with his need to stay busy, like a curious mind reaching for unknown boundaries. 'Just like him to always have his nose in a book even during lunch breaks', he thought.

"But it's not always just work and school, right?" Winston asked. "You also attend those parties out in the campground, yeah?" There had been a big one on the night of the murder.

Addison picked the book off the table and flipped through the pages, shrugging nonchalantly. "Yeah, I was there. So was half the town. Doesn't mean I know anything about what happened to Ernest. That party was big, a lot could've happened."

Next to Addison, Winston noticed an array of tools lined up on the workbench. Screwdrivers, hammers, and a crowbar among others, which was casually left on the side of the workbench. He'd seen Addison regularly with his work tools, it was part of being an apprentice.

"So, you're a mechanic apprentice, right?" Winston asked. "You work with these kinds of tools every day?"

Addison looked at him for a moment before nodding. "That's right. It's my field of work. Handling tools like crowbars is just part of the job."

Winston left Addison with his book and his workshop, making his way out to his car.

Camping, tool handling, busy campgrounds... Winston had a lot to think about on the drive back to the station. But, as always, the detective knew better than to rush to any conclusions just yet. The only thing certain was that everyone he met added a new piece to the puzzle. That was the nature of his job,⟦ chasing⟧ the truth and sifting through the fragments of life his line of work offered him. Little by little, every witness, every suspect, and every victim told their own part of the story.

Winston watched Octavia’s firm grip around her mug of lukewarm coffee. She was a sturdy woman, her experience in construction before joining the police force wasn't common knowledge, but it gave her that burly silhouette. He also knew that she had picked up a knack for handling construction tools, crowbars included, from her watch in the building business.

"Officer Octavia," started Winston, trying to appear casual, "Officer 'tavia," he corrected himself, as per the way locals referred to her, "you were on patrol the night Ernest was murdered, correct?"

Her gaze remained steady, not threatening nor hesitant, "Yes, that would be right."

"Were the campgrounds along your route?" asked Winston, knowing that he was treading on thin ice. The campgrounds which were part of her regular beat were also where poor Ernest was found dead.

"They sure were," she replied without diverting her gaze. "I've patrolled there for years now."

Winston pressed on, “Ernest, a known revealer of secrets, was threatening to leak his current findings. He'd uncovered an officer’s shady past and he claimed it was yours. Know anything about that?”

Octavia just looked through him, her facial muscles taut as she remained stoic. "Ernest was always digging around for information, but I can't say I do."

Staying strategic, he continued, "Ernest indicated that this officer with supposed shady practices was involved in illegal activities before joining the force. Oddly reminiscent of your own construction and police career, Octavia. Fearful of any skeletons in the closet that might be found?”

Here, Octavia's mask seemed to crack, but just for a moment, "I've no idea what you're implying."

Winston chose his next words carefully, conscious of her legal knowledge, “Do you have access to a crowbar, officer Octavia?”

She let out a short laugh, a sarcastic retort forming on her lips, “Well, every police department has its set of tools, Winston. Are you implying because we have crowbars, we might be swinging them at the locals?”

Winston remained silent, letting Octavia’s scoff hang in the air before speaking again. He gently changed the direction of his questions, “During your patrol last night, did you happen to see anything out of ordinary at the camp?”

“Just a quiet starry night, nothing too wild happening in my town, Winston.”

As the conversation winded up, Winston decided to leave Octavia with one last piece of thought, “Ernest had hinted at uncovering a cop's illegal past, may be yours. It does seem like there’s something you’d want to keep from the force.”

For the first time during their conversation, Octavia looked unsure. She shook her head, "I couldn't tell you, Winston."

As an investigative officer himself, Winston knew the camaraderie among the police ranks. Tonight he’d heard enough. He’d got Octavia talking, about her quiet patrol night and the secret that she urgently seemed to want buried, and her past involvement in illegal activities. As he left Octavia’s living room, he could not help but wonder more about this lady cop with a knack for using crowbars.<turn|>

In the wake of Lola's mysterious katana-driven demise at a secluded mountain cabin, Detective Winston finds himself entangled in a web of suspicion, with Isabelle and Frank peering anxiously from its corners.

In the tempered light of the police station, Detective Winston flipped open the file for his latest case. Pinned to the top was a grim photo of Lola, the victim, marking another life prematurely ended. A set of intimate text messages from Lola to another man caught his attention, reportedly found by Isabelle. Winston found the content of the messages interesting, adding more intrigue to the case. Lower in the pile, there was a picture of Isabelle, his prime suspect. 

With a dedication observed during her thrice weekly visits, Isabelle had become a familiar figure in her local dojo, her commitment noted by fellow practitioners. Winston dialed the dojo and had a brief but informative conversation with her sensei, before putting the phone back with a small sigh. Her sensei revealed that Isabelle had been seen sharpening her Katanas after each session.

David, Lola's life coach, had confided a lot in Isabelle, spending a considerable amount of time alone with her, a fact that Winston found odd. Isabelle had not only found some of Lola's intimate messages, but she had also seen Lola kissing the unknown man, making her knowledge even more suspect. The phone buzzed back into life, David at the other end of the line filling Winston in on his last intimate conversation with Isabelle. Their relationship was unconventional - it didn’t seem standard for a life coach to be so close to a friend of their clients.

“What brings you up here, Detective?” Isabelle asked when Winston arrived at her door. She was out of breath and had chalk dusted on her pants, evident either from her routine rock climbing training or her regular hike which she often indulged in.

Winston followed Isabelle into the house and entered a room solely dedicated to her Katana collection. Some were ornate, clearly for show, but others showed signs of recent care, with the wear marks from constant sharpening along the blade, the same the sensei had mentioned.

“So, you visit Lola’s mountain cabin often?” Winston asked, shifting the conversation. 

“Yeah, I’ve been up there a handful of times when Lola is alone. It’s quiet and at a considerable altitude, inaccessible without physical fitness, perfect to clear the mind,” Isabelle admitted. She described the layout of the cabin in detail, showing her familiarity with the place. But her voice seemed somewhat strained, the memory of seeing Lola and the man in an intimate exchange casting a shadow.

They talked a while longer about the trails to the cabin, which Winston rightly noted required considerable physical strength. The conversation then swung to David, and they spoke freely about their close, somewhat unconventional friendship.

Upon his return to the dojo, Winston observed the elegance and precision with which the sensei moved a katana. His mind drifted back to the crime scene, Lola’s body lying in an eerily tranquil way, as if her death had been executed by someone trained in a lethal art. 

Back in the car, Winston flicked his cigarette butt into the darkness, a chill passing over him as he thought of Lola, alone in the cabin at the time she was killed. What a dark sense of humor life had, he reflected, as he prepared to tackle the case.

As Winston paced the floor of his small and cluttered office, he reviewed his notes about Lola's murder. The whole scene of the gruesome act was set in a secluded mountain cabin, salted wounds for the peaceful surroundings. She had invited Frank for a work retreat, a secret invitation that he told no one about, and Winston decided that perhaps it was time to visit the suspect.

As a biologist, Frank was surrounded by microscopes and lab coats by the day, while his nights were spent in a dojo, practicing martial arts. Winston's curiosity piqued upon learning of his weapon of choice, the katana. 

Winston carefully examined Frank's martial arts record and noticed Frank's regularity in practicing with his katanas. A clue that Winston found interesting was the fact that Frank recently acquired a sharpening stone. An unusual purchase when you considered his profession.

Frank's laboratory colleagues had divulged that he often had a peculiar habit. He would abruptly leave work and colleagues found new insect bites on his skin afterwards. This could be nothing⟦ more⟧ than a biologist exploring his environment, but Winston had a gut feeling that there was more to it.

Winston had also come across Frank's bank statements, where funds were frequently withdrawn to flight booking sites. Odd for someone whose work seemed to revolve mostly around his lab, but not out of the ordinary either.

Frank's home had companion pets who were frequently ill during his unexplained absences. Curiously, this seemed to coincide with his unusual hobby of abruptly leaving his office and heading in the unknown, Winston made a mental note to investigate Frank's suspicious departures more closely.

On the day of Lola's murder, Frank's schedule had no entries. Couple that with an eye-witness account of him being seen near the mountain cabin and Winston decided it was time to reach out to this elusive biologist. As he dialed Frank's number, Winston knew that he was getting closer to unveiling the truth. "Mr. Frank," he said, "It's Detective Winston, let's talk."<turn|>
